evidence.excerpt:
Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-
step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing
benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR
agents' capabilities inreal-world life and professional productivitysettings insuffi-
ciently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LIFESEARCH, a challenging
benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query
seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. Specially, we spend totally
more than 4,500 hours of human annotation to construct over 4,000 expert-written,
fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy,
as well as concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct
extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation

Motivated by this gap, we present LIFESEARCH, a benchmark for evaluating DR agents on real-world
life and professional productivity search. We hired crowd workers to write the initial query seeds,
which undergo filtering and expert-guided refinement to form the benchmark tasks. LIFESEARCH
spans 7 concrete life and productivity domains, and its construction involves more than 4,500 hours of
human labor to produce over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics that comprehensively assess
both the coverage and the accuracy of a candidate report. Specifically, LIFESEARCHcomprises
203 tasks: 102 in Chinese and 101 in English. A substantial fraction of our rubrics arenumeric
and grounded in concrete values, units, or thresholds. Satisfying these criteria therefore requires
retrieving and reporting the precise quantities rather than producing qualitatively plausible

Furthermore, we compare 11 LLM-judge configurations on 402 human-annotated rubric labels and
select Gemini 3.1 Pro with low reasoning effort and zero temperature for benchmark grading. A
human ranking study shows that the overall rankings produced by our evaluation closely agree with
human rankings, yielding Spearman'sρ= 0.89and Kendall'sτ= 0.81.
We evaluate 12 frontier DR agents under a shared harness (Figure 1), yielding three main findings.i)
Substantial headroom remains:Even top-performing GPT-5.6 Sol reaches only 63.4%, with all
systems falling below 70% across domains.ii) Quality transcends volume:Higher scores correlate
with longer reports, yet volume alone is non-deterministic: Claude Opus 5 and GLM-5.3 have
comparable token counts but differ by 6.9 percentage points, highlighting the centrality of evidence
synthesis.iii) Common failure modes:Autonomous runs can fail

We adopt a rubric-based LLM-as-a-Judge approach to assess each final report. The resulting rubric-
level judgments are aggregated into a score.
Given a task, its rubric set, and a candidate report, an LLM judge assigns a binary Pass/Fail label to
each rubric. Judgments follow the rubric's acceptance conditions, including factual targets, source
requirements, and temporal scope. Semantically equivalent wording and numerical approximations
are accepted where permitted by the rubric. Let Rq denote the rubric set for task q, and let yq,r ∈

importance within the task. We first normalize the weighted satisfaction score within each task and

evidence.excerpt:
For judge selection in the DR rubric setting, we annotate one anonymized model response for each
of 20 tasks (10 Chinese, 10 English), covering 402 rubrics. For each report, two to three domain
experts independently assign binary Pass/Fail labels, reaching a substantial inter-annotator agreement
(mean pairwise Cohen's κ= 0.715). All 65 initial disagreements are subsequently resolved through
discussion to form the reference labels used to compare judge configurations.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The LLM judge is calibrated against 402 human reference rubric labels, and aggregate benchmark scores are corroborated by a human ranking study over 210 reports showing strong rank agreement.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Scoring against 4,014 expert-annotated rubrics using Gemini 3.1 Pro (low reasoning, zero temperature) as an LLM judge.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: None; the 12 evaluated frontier agents are third-party systems run out of the box in a unified ReAct harness without benchmark-specific training, tuning, or rubric-targeted optimization.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding current agent performance limits (top model GPT-5.6 Sol achieving 63.4%) and the non-deterministic relationship between report volume and quality are well-supported by experimental data and domain breakdowns.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The authors benchmark 12 frontier DR agents within a standardized harness across three independent runs, capturing resource usage and error patterns. Benchmark grading is corroborated by human inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.715), judge accuracy validation (84.25%), and a report-level human ranking study showing high rank correlation (Spearman rho = 0.89, Kendall tau = 0.81).

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Judge decisions are validated against 402 human reference rubric labels, and aggregate benchmark scores are corroborated by a human preference ranking study over 210 reports across 7 systems.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Scoring against 4,014 fine-grained rubrics using Gemini 3.1 Pro (low reasoning, zero temperature) as an LLM judge.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: None; evaluated frontier models are third-party systems tested out of the box in a unified ReAct harness without benchmark-specific fine-tuning or rubric-targeted optimization.

primary.limitations: The authors identify model-level failure modes (premature termination, temporal violations, missing details) and report the evaluation window constraints.
primary.method_assessment: The construction methodology combines crowdsourced query collection, multi-stage LLM-assisted filtering/rewriting, and expert refinement into subtasks with grounded, weighted rubrics. Judge model selection is transparently evaluated across 11 LLM-judge configurations against consensus human labels.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents a rigorous benchmark for deep research agents with thorough documentation of dataset curation, rubric design, judge calibration against human ground truth, and extensive cross-model evaluation.
primary.scoped_contribution: LifeSearch is an evaluation benchmark targeting deep research (DR) agents in real-world life and professional productivity contexts, containing 203 bilingual tasks (Chinese and English) and 4,014 expert-annotated fine-grained rubrics.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents a rigorous benchmark for deep research agents with thorough documentation of dataset curation, rubric design, judge calibration against human ground truth, and extensive cross-model evaluation.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors identify model-level failure modes (premature termination, temporal violations, missing details) and report the evaluation window constraints.

limitations_or_uncertainty.value: Structured research-card claims use title, abstract/summary, metadata, screening rules, and curation. A separate scholarly-quality assessment used bounded full-text excerpts, but unsupported claim, method, or evidence fields remain unextracted.
